tagline: Up the Black Creek Valley, over to the canyon's mouth.
intro: From Lupton on the interstate, Navajo Route 12 runs north up the Black Creek Valley through Window Rock and Fort Defiance, then slips into New Mexico at the town of Navajo, where a sawmill opened in 1960 with 300 Navajo workers. North of there the Navajo forest of the Chuska Mountains keeps the road company toward Tsaile.

At Tsaile Route 64 turns west, and Canyon del Muerto runs along the south side of the road the rest of the way to Chinle. The whole road is about 100 miles, and in 2001 it was renamed Diné Tah, among the people.

moments.title: Window Rock
moments.text: Named for its sandstone window. John Collier proposed the ceremonial name, Center of the World, and Navajos soon made a joke of it.

moments.title: Tsaile
moments.text: Diné College, the first college founded by Native Americans for Native Americans, chose this spot for its water, forests and lakes, and put up most of its buildings eight-sided like a hogan.

moments.title: Chinle
moments.text: The name means flowing out, for the water leaving Canyon de Chelly. A trader here was putting up tourists bound for the canyon by 1915.
